summary: A second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic for schizophrenia and bipolar mania. It is less likely than many similar medicines to cause weight and cholesterol problems, but it can change heart rhythm (QT prolongation), so ECG safety matters, and it must be taken with a real meal (at least 500 calories) to work properly.
description: Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic used for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (manic or mixed episodes). Given as a muscle injection, it can calm severe agitation quickly; taken by mouth, it can stabilize manic symptoms. The big catch: it can lengthen the QT interval (a heart-rhythm change seen on an ECG), and it is only absorbed well if you take it with food, at least 500 calories. It tends to cause less weight gain and fewer cholesterol problems than some other antipsychotics, but sleepiness, dizziness, a strong inner restlessness and other movement side effects can still happen.
patient_summary: Ziprasidone (Geodon) is an atypical antipsychotic for schizophrenia and bipolar mania. As an injection it can work fast for agitation, and taken by mouth it helps stabilize mania. You must take the capsules with a meal (at least 500 calories) or you may not absorb enough medicine. The biggest safety issue is a heart-rhythm change (QT prolongation — seen on an ECG), so ECGs and blood salt levels matter. Compared with some other antipsychotics, it usually causes less weight gain and fewer cholesterol problems.

primary.context: FDA-approved for schizophrenia. Oral dosing requires taking with a meal (≥500 calories) to ensure reliable absorption.
FDA-approved for manic or mixed episodes. Often used when weight and metabolic side effects are a big concern, but heart-rhythm (QT) risk must be checked.

secondary.context: IM formulation is labeled for acute agitation in schizophrenia when rapid control is needed and IM antipsychotic use is appropriate.

off_label.context: Sometimes added to an antidepressant for depression that has not responded to treatment, or for depression with loss of touch with reality (hearing or believing things others don't) (off-label).
Used short-term as an add-on in intensive care for delirium with distressing agitation or anxiety that continues despite non-medicine and medical care (off-label).
May be used for delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis), raising the dose slowly to the lowest dose that works (off-label).

therapeutic_response.display: IM agitation: initial effects within ~15 minutes; adequate calming within ~30 minutes

common_adverse_effects.notes: Expect possible sleepiness, especially early. If it wipes you out, that’s a dosing/timing conversation—not a personal failure. Safety first: driving, ladders, and sharp decisions can wait until you know how you respond.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Movement side effects (stiffness, shaking or restlessness)
common_adverse_effects.notes: EPS can look like stiffness, tremor, restlessness, dystonia, or subtle swallowing problems. If you feel “off” in your muscles or you’re pacing nonstop, say it early—there are ways to adjust.

common_adverse_effects.effect: A strong inner restlessness, hard to sit still
common_adverse_effects.notes: This is not just anxiety. It’s a whole-body restlessness that can be miserable and add to distress. Don’t just push through it; it is treatable and often linked to the dose.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness, or feeling faint when standing up
common_adverse_effects.incidence: 3% to 16% (dizziness); drops in blood pressure on standing reported
common_adverse_effects.notes: Dizziness is most likely while the dose is being raised. Drink fluids, stand up slowly, and tell your clinician if you faint or nearly faint. Falls are a big deal, especially in older adults.
Taking with food helps absorption and can help nausea. If nausea is persistent, timing and dose adjustments can help.

serious_risks.risk: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes (rare, higher risk with multiple risk factors): palpitations, syncope, sudden collapse—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
A rare emergency (NMS): very high fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, swings in blood pressure, heart rate or sweating. This is a medical emergency; get help right away.
Severe hypersensitivity reactions (including DRESS or Stevens-Johnson syndrome): rash with fever, swelling, mucosal lesions—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe EPS complications: dysphagia/aspiration risk, especially in medically fragile or older adults.
Blood count problems (rare): a dangerous drop in white blood cells (infection risk). Get checked if you have repeated infections, fevers or a sore throat.
Severe metabolic complications (rare): significant hyperglycemia, hyperosmolar states—seek care for excessive thirst/urination, confusion.

safety.black_box_warning: Higher risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis: older adults with dementia-related psychosis who take antipsychotic medicines have a higher risk of death. Ziprasidone is not approved to treat dementia-related psychosis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to ziprasidone or any component
Taking other medicines that lengthen the QT interval at the same time (including class Ia/III heart-rhythm medicines and other high-risk QT medicines)
Concurrent use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of discontinuing an MAOI (including linezolid and IV methylene blue)

precautions: Heart-rhythm change (QT prolongation — seen on an ECG) that grows with the dose: avoid it if your QT interval is already long or you have major risk factors for QT prolongation
If your QTc (heart-rhythm measure) goes above about 500 msec or rises a lot during treatment, the dose may need to be lowered or you may need to switch to a different antipsychotic
Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure): fainting and fall risk, especially while the dose is being raised
A rare but life-threatening reaction (NMS): fever, rigid muscles, confusion, swings in blood pressure, heart rate or sweating
Movement side effects (stiffness, shaking or restlessness) can occur, including a strong inner restlessness
Temperature dysregulation: higher risk with dehydration, heat exposure, strenuous exercise
Not indicated for catatonia and may worsen risk (including NMS) if catatonia is present
Suicide risk exists in severe mental illness; prescribe the smallest practical quantity and monitor closely early in treatment

interactions.mechanism: The effects on heart rhythm (QT) add up, raising the risk of torsades (a dangerous heart rhythm), especially with several risk factors.
interactions.action: Avoid combining whenever possible. If unavoidable, do it with a plan: baseline ECG, electrolyte correction (K/Mg/Ca), and follow-up ECG after dose changes.

interactions.interactant: Class Ia and Class III antiarrhythmics (eg, quinidine/procainamide; amiodarone/sotalol/dofetilide/ibutilide)
interactions.action: Avoid the combination; the label says ziprasidone should not be used with many medicines that lengthen the QT interval.

interactions.mechanism: Low potassium or magnesium increases QT/TdP risk.
interactions.action: Correct electrolytes before treatment when clinically relevant; monitor electrolytes in at-risk patients (vomiting/diarrhea, diuretics, poor intake).

interactions.interactant: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, alcohol, other sedatives)
interactions.mechanism: More sedation, dizziness, impaired coordination → falls and functional impairment.
interactions.action: Use caution, start lower, and monitor alertness/falls risk. Don’t stack sedating meds casually.

interactions.interactant: Food (this is an interaction, not a suggestion)
interactions.mechanism: Without a meal ≥500 calories, exposure drops and the medication may underperform.
interactions.action: Take every oral dose with a real meal (≥500 calories). Make it automatic—tie dosing to breakfast and dinner.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: ECG and heart-rhythm (QT) risk: checked before starting when needed (risk factors, heart history, interacting medicines), and again after big dose increases or when adding medicines that affect QT. Report a pounding heartbeat or fainting right away.
Electrolytes: Correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia/hypocalcemia when clinically relevant; electrolyte disturbances raise QT/TdP risk.
Vitals and orthostatics: Especially early in treatment and after dose changes. Falls risk matters—don’t ignore dizziness.
Sedation/alertness: Every visit. Screen for daytime sleepiness and functional impairment (driving/work/school).

Movement side effects, restlessness and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that can last): asked about every visit, with a formal rating scale at least once a year (or every 6 months if high risk)
Metabolic monitoring: Weight/BMI (early and ongoing), fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipid panel—ziprasidone is usually lower-risk but monitoring still applies.
Prolactin hormone effects: questions about symptoms (sexual problems, period changes, milky nipple discharge, breast growth in men); levels checked if you have symptoms
Blood count (CBC): when needed, especially if you have had low white blood cells before, including from a medicine
Adherence and food requirement: Every visit. If it “isn’t working,” first question is: Are you taking it with ≥500 calories?

special_populations.pregnancy: Newer (second-generation) antipsychotics as a group have not shown a large, consistent increase in major birth defects, but data for individual medicines vary and long-term effects on child development are still limited. Use in the last three months of pregnancy can cause movement or withdrawal symptoms in the newborn (agitation, feeding problems, abnormal muscle tone, breathing trouble, sleepiness, shaking). Decisions should be made together, aiming for the lowest dose that works and avoiding extra medicines when possible. Do not stop a treatment that is working just because of pregnancy if the risk of relapse is high.
special_populations.lactation: Ziprasidone is present in breast milk in limited case-report data, with a reported relative infant dose around ~1.2% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose in one report. Outcome data are limited. If breastfeeding during ziprasidone treatment is chosen, monitor the infant for excess sedation, irritability, poor feeding, and abnormal movements (EPS). Use the lowest effective dose and avoid stacking sedating meds when possible.
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid for behavior symptoms of dementia or delirium unless non-medicine options have failed and there is a risk of harm. For schizophrenia or bipolar disorder in older adults, start at the lower end of adult dosing, raise the dose slowly, and watch closely for sleepiness, dizziness on standing and falls, heart-rhythm (QT) changes, and low blood sodium (which can cause confusion, headache or seizures). Antipsychotics are potentially inappropriate in adults 65 and older for dementia-related behavior symptoms because of the risk of stroke and death.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No dose change is usually needed for the capsules or injection with kidney problems. The injection contains cyclodextrin, which may build up with repeated doses in people with kidney problems; how much this matters is unclear, so repeated injections should be used with caution.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: The manufacturer gives no formal dose change, but the liver breaks down most of the medicine and levels may rise. Use with caution if you have liver problems, watching for side effects and heart-rhythm (QT) risk.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism; primarily via non-CYP pathways (glutathione and aldehyde oxidase); CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 contribute to a smaller portion
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: A meal ≥500 calories can increase exposure by ~80%; without food, absorption can be unreliable

dosing.titration: Ziprasidone dosing depends on the target problem (schizophrenia, bipolar mania, or acute agitation) and the route (oral vs IM). Oral doses must be taken with a meal (≥500 calories) for reliable absorption.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If ziprasidone needs to be stopped (side effects, lack of benefit, switching meds), the safest path is usually a gradual taper—unless you’re stopping because of a serious adverse event that requires immediate discontinuation. Abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal-style symptoms and a rebound of the underlying illness.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Ziprasidone (Geodon) is an atypical antipsychotic used for {link:condition:schizophrenia:schizophrenia} and for acute manic or mixed episodes in {link:condition:bipolar-disorder:bipolar disorder}. It can also be given IM for rapid control of acute agitation when psychosis is driving the agitation. The tradeoff is QTc risk (heart rhythm) and the fact that oral doses only work reliably if you take them with a real meal (≥500 calories).
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Reduces hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, agitation related to psychosis
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar disorder (mania/mixed episodes)}: Helps bring down manic energy, irritability, racing thoughts, impulsivity
{link:condition:acute-agitation:Acute agitation (IM)}: Rapid calming when an IM antipsychotic is appropriate
off_label: Adjunctive treatment for major depressive disorder (treatment-resistant or with psychotic features)

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It didn’t change who I am—it just turned down the intensity.
My brain stopped sprinting. I could finally sit still.
The rage-y edge softened enough for me to think before I reacted.
I felt sleepy and kind of heavy the first week.
It calmed me down, but I also felt slowed down.
If I took it and then tried to do life… nope. Not at first.
items.note: Sedation is common, especially early or with dose increases.

quotes: I wasn’t anxious mentally, but my body felt like it couldn’t stop moving.
I kept pacing and didn’t know why—super uncomfortable.
It helped my thoughts, but the restlessness was the dealbreaker.
items.note: Akathisia can feel like internal motor anxiety. It’s a real side effect, not “just you.”

quotes: When I skipped food, it felt like I took nothing.
I had to plan my day around meals, which was annoying but necessary.
Once I started taking it with a real meal, it finally felt consistent.
items.note: Without enough calories, absorption drops and people often think the medication “doesn’t work.”

quotes: I didn’t gain a ton of weight like I did on other meds.
My appetite didn’t explode, which was a relief.
It felt more ‘neutral’ on my body compared to the heavy hitters.
items.note: Ziprasidone tends to have lower weight and lipid risk than many other SGAs, but monitoring still matters.

sections.intro: Ziprasidone can feel like a “volume knob” on agitation, mania, and psychosis—when it’s the right fit. But it has a very specific personality: it’s picky about food, and it’s picky about your heart rhythm (QTc).

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: How fast ziprasidone works depends on the form (IM vs oral) and what you’re treating (agitation vs mania vs schizophrenia).
key_points: IM agitation: Initial effects can show up within ~15 minutes; adequate calming often within ~30 minutes
Oral schizophrenia: Early improvement may show up in 1-2 weeks, with continued gains over 4-6 weeks
Oral acute mania: Some people notice changes within days, with clearer improvement over 1-2 weeks
Oral depression adjunct (off-label): Some people notice changes within ~1 week; fuller effect may take 6-12 weeks
Half-life (oral): ~7 hours in adults, so it’s typically dosed twice daily

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: With ziprasidone, success usually looks like fewer psychotic symptoms (less paranoia, fewer hallucinations), less manic activation (less racing, impulsivity, agitation), and better day-to-day function—without intolerable sedation, restlessness, or QTc issues. The key is taking it with enough food and tracking side effects early so you’re not suffering silently.
sections.clinical_details: Ziprasidone is an effective antipsychotic for schizophrenia and an antimanic agent for bipolar mania/mixed episodes, but it’s often selected for a specific profile: lower metabolic burden than some SGAs, with the tradeoff of higher QTc-prolongation risk and the strict food requirement for oral dosing.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: QTc prolongation risk: ziprasidone can affect heart rhythm. ECG safety is not optional—especially if you have risk factors.
sections.black_box: Increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis: older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Ziprasidone is not approved for the treatment of dementia-related psychosis.
other: Dose-dependent QTc interval prolongation: avoid if baseline QTc is prolonged or if you have major risk factors for QT prolongation
If QTc exceeds ~500 msec or rises markedly on treatment, lowering the dose or switching to a different antipsychotic may be necessary
Orthostatic hypotension: dizziness, fainting, fall risk—especially during titration
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare but life-threatening): fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability
Extrapyramidal symptoms (movement side effects) can occur, including akathisia
Temperature dysregulation: higher risk with dehydration, heat exposure, strenuous exercise
Not indicated for catatonia and may worsen risk (including NMS) if catatonia is present
Suicide risk exists in severe mental illness; prescribe the smallest practical quantity and monitor closely early in treatment
patient_counseling: Take every oral dose with a meal (≥500 calories). If you don’t, absorption can drop and the medication may feel inconsistent or ineffective.
Tell your clinician if you’ve ever had fainting, a known long-QT diagnosis, heart failure, a recent heart attack, or a history of abnormal rhythms.
Avoid stacking QT-prolonging meds. Bring a full med list (including antibiotics/antiemetics) to every visit.
If you feel severe dizziness, palpitations, chest pain, or you faint—treat it as urgent and get medical help.
Stand up slowly during titration. Hydrate. Falls happen most when people push through dizziness like it’s nothing.
If you get high fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, or drenching sweats—this can be an emergency (possible NMS).
If you develop intense restlessness (can’t sit still), speak up early—akathisia can be treated, but you shouldn’t just suffer.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common issues include drowsiness/somnolence, dizziness, headache, nausea, and movement side effects (EPS/akathisia). Metabolic effects (weight/lipids/glucose) are generally lower than some other SGAs, but not zero. QTc prolongation is the signature safety concern.
plain_language_list: Movement side effects (stiffness, tremor, dystonia—less common but possible)
Weight gain (possible, usually lower risk than some other antipsychotics)
Heart rhythm changes (QTc prolongation)—rarely dangerous, but the risk matters

common.patient_note: Expect possible sleepiness, especially early. If it wipes you out, that’s a dosing/timing conversation—not a personal failure. Safety first: driving, ladders, and sharp decisions can wait until you know how you respond.
EPS can look like stiffness, tremor, restlessness, dystonia, or subtle swallowing problems. If you feel “off” in your muscles or you’re pacing nonstop, say it early—there are ways to adjust.
Akathisia is not just anxiety. It’s a body-level agitation that can be miserable and can increase distress. Don’t white-knuckle it—this is treatable and often dose-related.
Dizziness is most likely during titration. Hydrate, stand slowly, and tell your clinician if you’re fainting or nearly fainting. Falls are a big deal—especially in older adults.
Taking with food helps absorption and can help nausea. If nausea is persistent, timing and dose adjustments can help.

serious: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes (rare, higher risk with multiple risk factors): palpitations, syncope, sudden collapse—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare): high fever, severe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe hypersensitivity reactions (including DRESS or Stevens-Johnson syndrome): rash with fever, swelling, mucosal lesions—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe EPS complications: dysphagia/aspiration risk, especially in medically fragile or older adults.
Blood count abnormalities (rare): leukopenia/neutropenia/agranulocytosis—seek evaluation for recurrent infections, fevers, sore throat.
Severe metabolic complications (rare): significant hyperglycemia, hyperosmolar states—seek care for excessive thirst/urination, confusion.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions

items.risk: Additive QTc prolongation → higher torsades risk, especially with multiple risk factors.
items.action: Avoid combining whenever possible. If unavoidable, do it with a plan: baseline ECG, electrolyte correction (K/Mg/Ca), and follow-up ECG after dose changes.

items.with: Class Ia and Class III antiarrhythmics (eg, quinidine/procainamide; amiodarone/sotalol/dofetilide/ibutilide)
items.action: Avoid combination; ziprasidone is contraindicated with many QT-prolonging agents per labeling.

items.risk: Low potassium or magnesium increases QT/TdP risk.
items.action: Correct electrolytes before treatment when clinically relevant; monitor electrolytes in at-risk patients (vomiting/diarrhea, diuretics, poor intake).

items.with: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, alcohol, other sedatives)
items.risk: More sedation, dizziness, impaired coordination → falls and functional impairment.
items.action: Use caution, start lower, and monitor alertness/falls risk. Don’t stack sedating meds casually.

items.with: Food (this is an interaction, not a suggestion)
items.risk: Without a meal ≥500 calories, exposure drops and the medication may underperform.
items.action: Take every oral dose with a real meal (≥500 calories). Make it automatic—tie dosing to breakfast and dinner.

sections.intro: Ziprasidone’s headline interaction problem is QTc. Anything that prolongs QT or raises arrhythmia risk can turn a manageable medication into a dangerous one. Food matters too: without enough calories, serum levels drop and efficacy becomes unreliable.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If ziprasidone needs to be stopped (side effects, lack of benefit, switching meds), the safest path is usually a gradual taper—unless you’re stopping because of a serious adverse event that requires immediate discontinuation. Abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal-style symptoms and a rebound of the underlying illness.
key_points: In chronic psychiatric illness, switching to another antipsychotic is often preferred over simply stopping, especially in schizophrenia where relapse risk is high.
If discontinuing by choice and not due to a major adverse event, taper over weeks to months when possible to watch for early relapse and reduce withdrawal reactions.
Possible withdrawal reactions include agitation, anxiety, sweating, GI symptoms, insomnia, irritability, tremor, dizziness/vertigo, dyskinesias, and rebound psychosis.
Switching strategies vary: cross-titration (most common), abrupt switch (sometimes), or overlap in high-relapse-risk patients while the new med reaches a therapeutic dose.
If QTc safety is the reason for stopping, the plan may prioritize rapid risk reduction while still protecting against psychiatric destabilization—this is specialist territory.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Ziprasidone dosing depends on the target problem (schizophrenia, bipolar mania, or acute agitation) and the route (oral vs IM). Oral doses must be taken with a meal (≥500 calories) for reliable absorption.

adult.schizophrenia_initial: 20 to 40 mg PO BID with meals (≥500 calories); for first-episode psychosis: 20 mg PO BID with meals
adult.schizophrenia_titration: Increase by 20 to 40 mg/day every ≥2 days based on response and tolerability; monitor for akathisia, orthostasis, sedation during titration
adult.schizophrenia_usual: 40 to 160 mg/day PO in 2 divided doses with meals
adult.bipolar_mania_initial: 40 mg PO BID with meals (≥500 calories)
adult.bipolar_mania_day2_adjustment: On day 2, may increase to 60 or 80 mg PO BID with meals
adult.bipolar_mania_usual: 40 to 80 mg PO BID with meals
adult.bipolar_mania_high_dose_note: Some people may require and tolerate doses up to 240 mg/day (specialist-level decision; QTc risk escalates with dose)
adult.maintenance_monotherapy: Continue the dose that controlled the acute episode (PO BID with meals)
adult.maintenance_adjunctive: 40 or 80 mg PO BID with meals (as adjunct to antimanic therapy)
adult.agitation_im_prn: IM: 10 mg every 2 hours OR 20 mg every 4 hours as needed; maximum 40 mg/day. Transition to oral as soon as possible
adult.delirium_oral_off_label: 20 to 40 mg PO every 12 hours with meals (if possible); maximum 80 mg/day
adult.delirium_im_off_label: IM: 10 mg then repeat every 2 hours as needed OR 20 mg then repeat once in 4 hours as needed; maximum 40 mg/day
adult.mdd_adjunct_off_label: 20 mg PO BID with meals; may increase by 40 mg/day each week up to 160 mg/day in 2 divided doses
adult.delusional_infestation_off_label: 20 mg PO BID with meals; increase gradually every few weeks to the lowest effective dose in the range of 20 to 80 mg PO BID; after response, maintain for 1 to 12 months before taper attempt

sections.simple_explanation: Oral ziprasidone is usually taken twice daily, and food is not optional—taking it with a meal (≥500 calories) can boost absorption dramatically. IM ziprasidone is for short-term rapid calming in acute agitation; it should be replaced by oral dosing as soon as clinically appropriate.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Ziprasidone can be used in pregnancy or postpartum when benefits outweigh risks, but decisions should be individualized and made together with you. Older adults need extra caution (falls, orthostasis, QTc risk), and ziprasidone is not approved for dementia-related psychosis due to increased mortality risk seen with antipsychotics in this population.
sections.pregnancy: Second-generation antipsychotics as a class have not shown a large, consistent increase in major congenital malformations, but data for individual agents vary and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes are still limited. Antipsychotic exposure in the third trimester can be associated with newborn EPS/withdrawal symptoms (agitation, feeding problems, abnormal tone, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Treatment decisions should be shared, focused on the lowest effective dose and avoiding polytherapy when possible. Do not stop effective treatment solely because someone is pregnant if the psychiatric relapse risk is high.
sections.lactation: Ziprasidone is present in breast milk in limited case-report data, with a reported relative infant dose around ~1.2% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose in one report. Outcome data are limited. If breastfeeding during ziprasidone treatment is chosen, monitor the infant for excess sedation, irritability, poor feeding, and abnormal movements (EPS). Use the lowest effective dose and avoid stacking sedating meds when possible.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for behavioral symptoms of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options have failed and there is risk of harm. For schizophrenia or bipolar disorder in older adults, start in the lower end of adult dosing, titrate slowly, and monitor closely for sedation, orthostatic hypotension/falls, QTc changes, and hyponatremia/SIADH risk. Antipsychotics are potentially inappropriate in adults ≥65 for dementia-related behavioral symptoms due to stroke and mortality risk.
sections.hepatic: No formal manufacturer dose adjustment, but ziprasidone undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and exposure may increase. Use with caution in hepatic impairment and monitor side effects and QTc risk.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is generally necessary for oral or IM ziprasidone in kidney impairment. IM formulation contains cyclodextrin, which may accumulate with repeated dosing in kidney impairment; clinical significance is unclear—use caution with repeated IM dosing in renal impairment.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: ECG/QTc risk: Baseline assessment when clinically indicated (risk factors, cardiac history, interacting meds). Recheck after significant dose increases or when adding QT-prolonging meds. Take QT complaints seriously (palpitations, syncope).
Electrolytes: Correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia/hypocalcemia when clinically relevant; electrolyte disturbances raise QT/TdP risk.
Vitals and orthostatics: Especially early in treatment and after dose changes. Falls risk matters—don’t ignore dizziness.
Sedation/alertness: Every visit. Screen for daytime sleepiness and functional impairment (driving/work/school).
EPS/akathisia and tardive dyskinesia: Ask every visit; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk).
Metabolic monitoring: Weight/BMI (early and ongoing), fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipid panel—ziprasidone is usually lower-risk but monitoring still applies.
Prolactin effects: Ask about symptoms (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia); check levels if symptomatic.
CBC: As clinically indicated, especially if you have had low WBC or drug-induced neutropenia before.
Adherence and food requirement: Every visit. If it “isn’t working,” first question is: Are you taking it with ≥500 calories?

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Ziprasidone comes as oral capsules and an IM formulation for acute agitation. Oral capsules should be swallowed whole and taken with food (≥500 calories). IM is for intramuscular use only (not IV).
items: Oral capsules: 20 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg, 80 mg (brand and generic)
IM injection (reconstituted solution): 20 mg vial (for IM use only)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Ziprasidone works by balancing dopamine and serotonin signaling in the brain. It blocks dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors (core antipsychotic effect), acts as an agonist at 5-HT1A, and also affects other serotonin receptors. It has some alpha-1 adrenergic blocking (which can contribute to dizziness/orthostasis) and moderate histamine-1 activity (which can contribute to sedation). It also moderately inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, which may matter for mood symptoms in some people.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Ziprasidone is often chosen when you want an effective antipsychotic/antimanic option with relatively lower risk of weight gain and lipid problems compared to some other SGAs, and you’re willing to manage the tradeoffs: QTc monitoring and the strict “take with ≥500 calories” rule. It can be a good fit if you prioritize metabolic safety and can reliably take it with meals. It may be a poor fit if you have cardiac risk, prolonged QTc or frequently missed meals, or can’t tolerate akathisia or sedation.

faqs.a: Ziprasidone is used to treat schizophrenia and acute manic or mixed episodes in bipolar disorder. The IM form can be used for rapid control of acute agitation when an IM antipsychotic is appropriate (commonly in agitation tied to psychosis).

faqs.q: Do I really have to take ziprasidone with food?
faqs.a: Yes. This is the most common reason it “doesn’t work.” A meal with at least 500 calories can increase absorption dramatically. If you take it without enough food, blood levels may be too low and symptoms can break through.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest safety concern with ziprasidone?
faqs.a: A heart-rhythm change called QT prolongation (seen on an ECG). Ziprasidone has a higher risk of this than many other atypical antipsychotics. It matters most if you already have a long QT, heart disease, low potassium or magnesium, or you take other medicines that lengthen the QT interval.

IM ziprasidone for acute agitation can start calming within about 15 minutes, with adequate calming often by ~30 minutes. Oral ziprasidone usually takes longer: schizophrenia improvement may begin in 1-2 weeks (with continued gains over 4-6 weeks), and mania can start improving within days to 1-2 weeks.

faqs.q: Is ziprasidone approved for dementia-related psychosis?
faqs.a: No. Like other antipsychotics, it carries a boxed warning about a higher risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, and ziprasidone is not approved for that use.

It can, but compared with some other atypical antipsychotics, ziprasidone is generally considered lower risk for major weight gain and lipid changes. That said, it’s not risk-free, so weight, glucose, and lipids should still be monitored.

faqs.q: What are common side effects people notice?
faqs.a: Sleepiness, dizziness, nausea, headache, and movement-related side effects (EPS) are common. Akathisia (a restless, can’t-sit-still feeling) can happen and should be addressed early.

faqs.q: Can ziprasidone be used for acute agitation?
faqs.a: Yes. The IM form can be used for acute agitation, especially when psychosis is suspected to be the primary driver. Typical IM dosing is 10 mg every 2 hours or 20 mg every 4 hours as needed (max 40 mg/day), with a plan to switch to oral as soon as possible.

faqs.q: How do I stop ziprasidone safely?
faqs.a: If you’re stopping because it’s not working or the side effects are too hard, the safest approach is usually to lower the dose slowly over weeks to months, unless a serious side effect means it must be stopped right away. Tapering helps reduce withdrawal-type symptoms (agitation, insomnia, sweating, stomach upset) and helps catch early relapse.
